paragraphs.heading: A bubble of magnetic space
paragraphs.text: A magnetosphere is the region of space around a planet or other body where that body's magnetic field acts on charged particles. It is created by an active dynamo inside the body. Near a planet with a dipole field, such as Earth, the field lines follow the simple pattern of a magnetic dipole. Farther out, they are pulled out of shape by the solar wind, a stream of electrically conducting plasma flowing from the Sun.

paragraphs.heading: Shield and early study
paragraphs.text: Planets with an active magnetosphere, Earth among them, can soften or block solar and cosmic radiation. Research on Earth's magnetosphere dates back to 1600, when William Gilbert showed that the field at the surface resembled that of a terrella, a small magnetized sphere. Elsasser proposed dynamo theory, which traces Earth's field to the motion of its iron outer core. Magnetometers then let scientists follow how the field changes over time and from place to place.

paragraphs.heading: The space age
paragraphs.text: In 1958 Explorer 1 was launched to measure cosmic rays above the atmosphere, and it found the Van Allen radiation belt in the inner magnetosphere; Explorer 3 confirmed the belt later that year. That same year Eugene Parker put forward the solar wind as an idea, and in 1959 Thomas Gold coined the word magnetosphere to describe how that wind meets Earth's field. In 1963, using data from Explorer 12, Cahill and Amazeen spotted a sudden drop in field strength near the noon meridian, later named the magnetopause. By 1983 the International Cometary Explorer had observed the distant magnetotail.

paragraphs.heading: Layers facing the solar wind
paragraphs.text: The outermost layer is the bow shock, the boundary between the magnetosphere and its surroundings, and around a planet the solar wind slows there as it nears the magnetopause. Inside it lies the magnetosheath, made mostly of shocked solar wind, where the field's strength and direction change erratically. The magnetosheath works like a cushion, passing the wind's pressure on to the planet's magnetic barrier. Next comes the magnetopause, where the push of the planet's field balances the push of the solar wind, and it changes size and shape as the wind's pressure rises and falls.

paragraphs.heading: The long tail
paragraphs.text: Opposite the squeezed part of the field, the magnetosphere stretches far beyond the planet in a magnetotail. The tail has a northern and a southern lobe: field lines in the northern lobe point toward the planet, and those in the southern lobe point away. The lobes are almost empty, holding few charged particles. Between them lies the plasma sheet, where the field is weaker and charged particles are packed more densely.

paragraphs.heading: Not every world has one
paragraphs.text: When a body's own magnetic field is what mainly holds off the solar wind, its magnetosphere is called intrinsic; Mercury, Earth, Jupiter, Ganymede, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are examples. When the field does not oppose the wind, the magnetosphere is called induced, and the wind meets the atmosphere, the ionosphere or the bare surface instead. Venus seems to lack an internal dynamo, so its only field forms as the solar wind wraps around the planet. Mars may fall in between, with both the planet and its field playing a part.
